titre: The 1913 Armory Show, Founding Scandal of American Modern Art
accroche: In 1913, New York discovers Cubism and mocks Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase. The scandal makes his career.
contenu_vulgarise:
On February 17, 1913, the Association of American Painters and Sculptors opens the International Exhibition of Modern Art at New York's 69th Regiment Armory: about one thousand three hundred works by more than three hundred American and European artists, a fifth of them women. Chaired by the painter Arthur B. Davies and organized by Walt Kuhn and Walter Pach, the show brings Impressionism, Fauvism, and Cubism together with American painting on this scale in the United States for the first time. The lawyer John Quinn, who delivers the opening address, uses the occasion to call for the removal of tariffs on imported modern art. The posters even announce, by mistake, the presence of Van Gogh and Cézanne, dead for twenty-three and seven years respectively.

## The painting no one can see

Among the works, one painting draws almost all the public's and the press's attention: *Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2*, painted the year before by Marcel Duchamp, a twenty-five-year-old Frenchman still unknown in the United States. Visitors look for the nude figure promised by the title and see only a sequence of geometric planes; in Chicago, a critic even holds a public lecture trying to locate her within the canvas. The New York Tribune's headline calls the show "A Remarkable Affair, Despite Some Freakish Absurdities." The most quoted line, "an explosion in a shingle factory," is attributed sometimes to the critic Julian Street, sometimes to the essayist Joel Spingarn: even the origin of the show's most famous joke is not established with certainty. The cartoonist J. F. Griswold publishes a parody in the New York Evening Sun titled *The Rude Descending a Staircase (Rush Hour at the Subway)*. The painting nonetheless, or perhaps because of all this, finds a buyer: the San Francisco dealer Frederic C. Torrey, the first American ever to own a work by Duchamp.

## Laughter as publicity

The exhibition then travels to the Art Institute of Chicago and the Copley Society in Boston, where the American works are removed for lack of space. In twenty-three days in Chicago, it draws about one hundred eighty-eight thousand visitors, more than New York's roughly eighty-seven thousand over its entire run: the New York scandal preceded the show and drew the crowds. Ridicule therefore does not hurt Duchamp's work, it makes it known: the most mocked canvas in the show becomes the most discussed, and the most discussed becomes the one people come to see. Duchamp settles in New York two years later and becomes a central figure of the American avant-garde, well before exhibiting a urinal signed *R. Mutt* there in 1917. The Armory Show did not convert the public to Cubism in a single season; it taught them, through laughter, that modern art existed, and that it was worth judging for themselves rather than only hearing about it.

carte.punch: In 1913, the most mocked painting at the Armory Show became the most talked about, then the best sold.
carte.idee: In New York in 1913, the public searches in vain for the nude figure in Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 and mocks it in the press. The scandal draws crowds in Chicago, where the show outdraws New York, and launches Duchamp's American career.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The detailed account of the exhibition, its organization, and its critical reception.
The story of the scandal and its 2013 centennial.

quiz.question: Why does Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 become the unwitting star of the 1913 Armory Show?
choix: Because it is the only work on display signed by an artist already famous in the United States
Because the show's jury awards it first prize before the exhibition opens to the public
Because it is the largest canvas on display, impossible to miss in the Armory's halls
Because the public and critics, unable to recognize a human figure in it, turn it into a target of mockery that draws the crowds
quiz.explication: The painting confuses viewers because no nude or staircase is recognizable at first glance; the press's mockery makes it the most talked-about work in the show, which draws in visitors who come to see what the fuss is about. Duchamp was unknown in the United States, and the work received no prize.
